topicSummaryParagraph: Infective endocarditis (IE) involves the colonization of heart valves or endocardial surfaces by pathogens. Subacute IE typically occurs on previously damaged valves (e.g., aortic stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, or mitral valve prolapse). The pathogenesis begins with turbulent blood flow causing focal endocardial injury, which triggers the deposition of sterile platelet-fibrin thrombi (nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis). During transient bacteremia, microorganisms adhere to these pre-existing thrombi. Culture-negative IE is often caused by fastidious organisms like Bartonella species (associated with homelessness or body lice), Coxiella burnetii, or the HACEK group, or it may occur following prior antibiotic use.

In patients with pre-existing valvular disease, turbulent blood flow damages the endocardium, exposing underlying extracellular matrix and triggering the formation of a sterile thrombus consisting of platelets and fibrin, known as nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE). During episodes of bacteremia, pathogens (like Viridans streptococci or Bartonella) adhere to these sterile vegetations.
